text: Dallas, the year 2000. Two young founders walk into blockbusters headquarters and offer to sell their tiny company for $50 million. Across the table, blockbusters CEO is trying very hard not to laugh. That tiny company was Netflix. Today, it's worth roughly $300 billion. And blockbuster? Its entire empire now fits inside one single store in a small town in Oregon. At its peak, Blockbuster made around $800 million a year from late fees alone. That's more than $2 million a day from people who forgot to return a movie. But here's what almost nobody tells you. Blockbuster didn't die because it ignored the internet. It saw it coming. It fought back. And for a moment, it was actually winning until a billionaire investor walked into the boardroom. Dallas, Texas, October 19, 1985. A man named David Cook opens a video rental store unlike anything people have seen. bright lights, wide aisles, around 8,000 tapes on the shelves and a computer system to check them out. Video stores back then were usually small, dark and a little sketchy. Blockbuster felt like a supermarket for movies. Then a businessman named Wayne Heisenga takes over and turns it into a machine. New stores everywhere. Make it a blockbuster night. Friday evening becomes a ritual. You walk the aisles, you fight your siblings over the box, and the one movie you actually wanted is always somehow rented out. Do you have the new Jurassic Park? All 40 copies are out. 40? 40. Want a documentary about bees? In 1994, the Media Giant Viacom buys blockbuster for $8.4 billion. By 2004, there are 9,094 blockbuster stores around the world and more than 84,000 employees. And here's the dirty secret of the business model. Late fees. Return your tape a day late and you pay. Blockbuster reportedly made about $800 million a year this way, roughly 16% of its revenue. Translation, $1 out of every six came from punishing its own customers. That's $4 for the rental. Great. And $8 of late fees. For a movie I didn't even like, especially for that one. Then came the red envelope. In 1997, two entrepreneurs in California read Hastings and Mark Randolph start a company that rent DVDs by mail. No store, no driving. You pick a movie on a website and it shows up in your mailbox. They call it Netflix. There's a famous legend that Hastings started Netflix out of rage after paying a $40 late fee on Apollo 13. Great story. But his co-founder later called it a convenient fiction. Basically branding. Very Hollywood. Still, in 2000 Netflix is losing money and needs help. So Hastings and Randolph fly to Dallas with an offer. Buy us for $50 million. You run the stores, will run the online business for you. According to Rand Off, Blockbuster's CEO John Antiochco was struggling not to laugh. The meeting went downhill fast. No deal. But here's the twist almost everyone forgets. Blockbuster wasn't ignoring the internet at all. That same year in July 2000, it signed a 20 year deal to stream movies over the internet. Its partner? A hot, innovative energy company from Houston called Enron. Yes, that Enron. Queue the ominous music. They tested it with about a thousand homes in four cities and by March 2001, eight months later, the 20 year deal was already over. A few months after that, Enron collapsed in one of the biggest frauds in American history. Blockbuster's first streaming partner, a company built on fake numbers. You can't make this up. And then Antioch O does something bold. In 2004, Blockbuster launches its own online rental service, Blockbuster Online. And on January 1st, 2005, it kills late fees, gone. Whew, just like that. a huge revenue stream thrown away on purpose to win back customers. Then in late 2006 comes the masterstroke. Total access. Rent DVDs online, like Netflix. But when you're done, drop them at any blockbuster store and walk out with a new movie instantly. Netflix had mailboxes, blockbuster had mailboxes and 9,000 stores. It works. By the end of 2006, blockbuster online has about 2 million subscribers. According to the book Netflix, new signups suddenly swing toward blockbuster. By the end of January 2007 Netflix's stock has dropped almost 12% for the first time the little red envelope is scared, picture it, the dinosaur is learning to fly. But then came the billionaire. Enter Carl Icon, one of Wall Street's most famous activist investors. Translation, someone who buys a big chunk of a company shares and then pressures management to do things his way. By 2005, he owns nearly 10% of blockbuster and wins 3 seats on the board. And icon hates the plan. The online service is expensive, killing late fees cost a fortune, and Tioco's bonus way too big according to icon. We're finally beating Netflix. Wonderful. How much is it costing us? A lot. Then stop beating them so expensively the fight gets ugly. And in 2007 Antiochal is out. His replacement is Jim Keys, the former boss of 7-Eleven. His priority paid down debt and bring focus back to the stores. Marketing for the online service gets cut. Growth stalls. Antiochal later said he believed Blockbuster Online could have reached 10 million subscribers if it had kept going. Meanwhile, in January 2007, Netflix quietly launches something new. Streaming. Watch instantly. No envelope. No store, no late fees, ever. You can probably guess the rest. September 23, 2010, Blockbuster files for bankruptcy with about $1.5 billion of debt. In 2011, the satellite TV company Dish buys what's left, including about 1700 stores in a deal valued at around $320 million. The stores close one after another until only one is left. Bend Oregon. By 2019, this is the last blockbuster store on the planet. And instead of disappearing, it becomes a tourist attraction. People fly in to take selfies by t-shirts, rent a DVD for old timescake. In 2020, the store was even listed on Airbnb for $4 a night. It got its own documentary and in 2026, it's still open. And Netflix, more than 300 million paying members, worth roughly $300 billion dollars the company blockbuster could have bought for 50 million So what's the lesson? Blockbuster didn't fail because it couldn't see the future. It saw it built it and was winning and then it chose short-term numbers over the long game Sometimes the most expensive decision isn't the one you refuse. It's the one you abandoned halfway. $50 million, one laugh, and the last laugh went to the red envelope. If you enjoyed this, subscribe.
